headline.text: The label reports faster methylphenidate release from extended-release capsules at 40% alcohol.

reported.text: For the pinned extended-release capsule, the label reports 84% methylphenidate release in the first hour at 40% alcohol.
In healthy volunteers ethanol with methylphenidate raised early plasma concentrations and potentiated high, good, like, stimulated and overall effect ratings.

pharmacistQuestions.text: The evidence here is limited. Is there anything about my health that makes this interaction more or less relevant?
Do any of my other medicines or products, like cough syrup or mouthwash, contain alcohol?
Does my dose, or the time between taking Methylphenidate and drinking alcohol, change how much this matters?

claims.text: The label states 40% alcohol increased methylphenidate release with 84% released in first hour.
claims.quote: At an alcohol concentration of 40%, there was an increase in the release rate of methylphenidate in the first hour, resulting in 84% of the methylphenidate being released.
claims.judgeRationale: The quote directly reports that 40% alcohol increased methylphenidate release, with 84% released in the first hour, matching the claim and pair exposure.

claims.text: Methylphenidate blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine into presynaptic neuron.
claims.quote: Methylphenidate blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine into the presynaptic neuron and increases the release of these monoamines into the extraneuronal space.
claims.judgeRationale: The quote describes methylphenidate monotherapy pharmacology without alcohol co-exposure, so it does not establish an alcohol-methylphenidate interaction mechanism.

claims.text: In 24 healthy volunteers, ethanol with dl-MPH raised early d-MPH plasma concentrations 44-99% versus dl-MPH alone.
claims.quote: Twenty-four healthy volunteers received dl-MPH (0.3 mg/kg) or d-MPH (0.15 mg/kg), with or without ethanol (0.6 g/kg). During the absorption phase of dl-MPH, concomitant ethanol significantly elevated d-MPH plasma concentrations (44-99%; P < 0.005).
claims.judgeRationale: The quote reports in 24 healthy volunteers that ethanol during dl-MPH absorption significantly elevated d-MPH concentrations by 44-99% versus the non-ethanol condition.

claims.text: In 24 healthy volunteers, ethanol with dl-MPH potentiated high, good, like, stimulated and overall effect.
claims.quote: Twenty-four healthy volunteers received dl-MPH (0.3 mg/kg) or d-MPH (0.15 mg/kg), with or without ethanol (0.6 g/kg). Furthermore, immediately following the ethanol drink the subjective effects of "high," "good," "like," "stimulated," and overall "effect" were significantly potentiated (P ≤ 0.01).

claims.text: In 24 healthy volunteers, ethanol raised d-MPH AUC 21% with dl-MPH and 14% with d-MPH.
claims.quote: Twenty-four healthy volunteers received dl-MPH (0.3 mg/kg) or d-MPH (0.15 mg/kg), with or without ethanol (0.6 g/kg). Ethanol increased the d-MPH area under the curve (AUC)(0-inf) by 21% following dl-MPH (P < 0.001) and 14% for d-MPH (P = 0.001).

claims.text: Findings consistent with l-MPH competitively inhibiting presystemic CES1 metabolism of d-MPH.
claims.quote: These findings are consistent with l-MPH competitively inhibiting presystemic CES1 metabolism of d-MPH.
claims.judgeRationale: The claim describes l-MPH inhibiting d-MPH metabolism without mentioning ethanol co-exposure, so it does not describe the alcohol-methylphenidate pair interaction.

claims.text: Ethanol with dl-MPH potentiated high, good, like, stimulated and overall effect ratings.
claims.quote: Twenty-four healthy volunteers received dl-MPH (0.3 mg/kg) or d-MPH (0.15 mg/kg), with or without ethanol (0.6 g/kg). During the absorption phase of dl-MPH, concomitant ethanol significantly elevated d-MPH plasma concentrations (44-99%; P < 0.005). Furthermore, immediately following the ethanol drink the subjective effects of "high," "good," "like," "stimulated," and overall "effect" were significantly potentiated (P ≤ 0.01). Plasma l-EPH concentrations exceeded those of l-MPH.
claims.judgeRationale: The quote reports that ethanol with dl-MPH significantly potentiated the subjective ratings of "high," "good," "like," "stimulated," and overall "effect," matching the claimed increased-effect interaction.

In a recent case, where a deceased person was found in his apartment, the police seized a plastic bag with the inscription \"ethylphenidate\". An autopsy of the 32-year-old man yielded a mitral valve endocarditis, which must have persisted a while before death, in combination with a pneumonia. At the Forensic Toxicological Centre (FTC) in Munich femoral blood, liver, pericardium fluid, urine, stomach content and hair of the deceased were analyzed for ethylphenidate after sample preparation by an LC-Triple TOF 5600. Calibration curves were spiked with a methanolic 1mg/mL solution of ethylphenidate (substance provided by the State Office of Criminal Investigation in Munich) in whole blood in comparison to liver and femoral blood, in serum in comparison to pericardium fluid and in urine in comparison to urine and stomach content, respectively. The present study tested the hypothesis that administration of the pure isomer dexmethylphenidate (d-MPH) will overcome the influence of ethanol on d-MPH absorption by eliminating competitive CES1-mediated presystemic metabolism of l-MPH to l-EPH. Twenty-four healthy volunteers received dl-MPH (0.3 mg/kg) or d-MPH (0.15 mg/kg), with or without ethanol (0.6 g/kg). During the absorption phase of dl-MPH, concomitant ethanol significantly elevated d-MPH plasma concentrations (44-99%; P < 0.005).
